args.body:
PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
PREPARED FOR CLIENT — ARBITRATION INTERNATIONAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION

MEMORANDUM

TO: Client — Arbitration International Dispute Resolution Matter
FROM: Counsel
RE: Counterparty Markup of the Arbitration Agreement — Analysis and Accept/Reject/Counter Recommendations
DATE: [Matter File Date]

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

We have reviewed the counterparty's second-round redline of the arbitration agreement (the "Counterparty Markup") against the original draft in our base deal materials, the governing SPA excerpts, and our internal arbitration/dispute-resolution drafting playbook. This memorandum identifies every deviation introduced by the counterparty, reconciles each against the governing schedules and exhibits that control over generalized language, applies the controlling deal-team instruction on negotiation priorities, and sets forth our recommendation to accept, reject, or counter each point.

Our analysis is grounded in the operative instruments for this engagement: (a) the original draft arbitration agreement (base deal materials); (b) the governing SPA excerpts and disclosure schedules (Schedule 3.7 and Schedule 5.2) and Exhibit B (survival matrix); (c) the Counterparty Markup (the revisions under review); and (d) the deal-team correspondence reflecting, as its controlling final message, the partner's revised negotiation priorities. We note, for completeness, that certain administrative correspondence was misfiled into the matter file; that material concerns a different engagement and has not been relied upon in any respect.

II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS

The Counterparty Markup accepts most firm-standard and SPA-consistent provisions but introduces three material deviations. Two of these — the indemnification cap reduction and the new limitation period shortening survival for the core representations — are unacceptable as drafted and must be rejected or countered. One — the conversion of the indemnity basket from a deductible to a tipping basket — is acceptable and the client has instructed that it be conceded. The MAE carve-out deviation requires careful reconciliation against Schedule 3.7 and should be rejected to the extent it expands beyond the already-disclosed regulatory inquiries.

Recommendations at a glance:
1. Indemnification cap reduction — REJECT / COUNTER (restore full cap); failure to do so shifts Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities to client.
2. Basket conversion (deductible → tipping) — CONCEDE per controlling partner instruction.
3. MAE regulatory carve-out — REJECT / NARROW to mirror only the two Schedule 3.7-disclosed inquiries.
4. Survival-period reduction for core representations — REJECT / WALK-AWAY trigger per controlling instruction; contradicts Exhibit B survival matrix.

III. BASE MATERIALS AND GOVERNING FRAMEWORK

A. Original Draft and SPA Excerpts. The operative arbitration agreement is part of the broader transaction documented by the SPA. The indemnification mechanics, MAE definition, and survival terms of the arbitration agreement must remain consistent with, and be read against, the SPA's Article VIII indemnification framework and its related disclosure schedules. The scheduled exceptions are determinative where they conflict with general statement language.

B. Governing Schedules and Exhibits.
- Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that are the precise subject matter of the counterparty's proposed MAE carve-out. Because schedule exceptions control over general language, the carve-out can only be accepted to the extent limited to these two disclosed matters, and not as a broader, open-ended exception.
- Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities. The counterparty's simultaneous reduction of the indemnification cap and conversion of the basket would, in combination with Schedule 5.2, silently shift these retained liabilities onto the client. The cap reduction must therefore be rejected to preserve the position that Schedule 5.2 liabilities remain seller-retained and fully indemnifiable.
- Exhibit B sets the survival matrix. The counterparty's proposed new limitation period directly contradicts Exhibit B's survival schedule for the core representations. Because Exhibit B is a controlling exhibit, the counterparty's survival reduction is inconsistent with the governing transaction documents.

C. Internal Playbook. Our internal arbitration/dispute-resolution playbook requires that any deviation from the agreed survival matrix, established MAE definition, and indemnity structure be identified and negotiated, with deviations from core risk allocations (particularly survival and indemnity caps) escalated. The playbook favors market-standard risk allocation for core representations and does not support the counterparty's requested modifications.

D. Controlling Deal-Team Instruction. The final (controlling) message in the deal-team correspondence revises the negotiation priorities: the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. This instruction supersedes earlier, opposite priority statements in the same thread and controls our recommendations.

IV. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduced and Basket Converted from Deductible to Tipping Basket

Description. The Counterparty Markup silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the indemnity basket from a deductible structure to a tipping basket.

Analysis. Reducing the cap alters the core economic allocation of the transaction. Read together with Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), the lower cap would cap seller exposure below the value of the retained liabilities disclosed on Schedule 5.2, effectively shifting those liabilities to the client beyond the contemplated cap. The capped liability amount is a defining risk term that SPA excerpts and the playbook treat as a seller-side core allocation; there is no disclosed basis in the schedules for the reduction.

On the basket, separately, conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket means that once the threshold is crossed the seller pays 100% of the losses (rather than only amounts above the deductible). This is a pro-buyer, market-common accommodation.

Recommendation.
- Cap: REJECT the silent cap reduction and COUNTER to restore the full cap reflected in the original draft and the SPA. The cap must remain at least sufficient to cover Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities; otherwise those liabilities would be shifted to the client without a corresponding price adjustment. This is a core risk-allocation term not supported by any schedule or playbook deviation.
- Basket: CONCEDE the deductible-to-tipping conversion, consistent with the controlling partner instruction. No counter is needed.

DEVIATION 2 — MAE Definition Adds Carve-Out for Regulatory Action of the Kind at Issue

Description. The Counterparty Markup adds a new carve-out to the Material Adverse Effect definition for "regulatory action of the kind at issue in this matter."

Analysis. The MAE definition is qualified by Schedule 3.7, which already discloses two pending regulatory inquiries of precisely this character. The carve-out as drafted is not limited to those two disclosed inquiries but purports to exclude a general category of "regulatory action of the kind at issue," which is broader than and inconsistent with the governing disclosure schedule. Under the deal materials, scheduled exceptions control over general statements; an expansive, open-ended carve-out therefore cannot be reconciled with the base materials, and it would operate to excuse MAEs arising from regulatory events that were never disclosed or bargained for.

Recommendation. REJECT the carve-out in its sweeping form and COUNTER to limit it to mirror exactly the two inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7. If the counterparty insists on the carve-out, it must be tied precisely to the two disclosed inquiries and time-limited to the survival period reflected in Exhibit B. This comports with both the playbook (no expansion of MAE carve-outs beyond disclosed matters) and the controlling schedules.

DEVIATION 3 — New Limitation Period Shortens Survival for the Core Representations

Description. The Counterparty Markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations.

Analysis. Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for all representations, including the core representations. The counterparty's proposed shorter limitation period directly contradicts Exhibit B. The deal-team correspondence establishes that any survival-period reduction is treated as a walk-away issue by the client and that this instruction controls. A shortened survival period would materially erode the client's post-closing remedies for breach of the core representations and would be inconsistent with both the controlling Exhibit B and the firm's market-standard position for core reps. This is a non-negotiable risk term.

Recommendation. REJECT the survival-period reduction categorically. Because the controlling instruction treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue, we should not offer a counter that retains any reduction. Restore the survival period for the core representations to Exhibit B. If the counterparty persists, we are instructed to treat this as a deal-breaker and escalate to a walk-away posture rather than concede.

V. RECONCILIATION AND OVERALL STRATEGY

The three deviations must be read together as a package. The combination of (i) a reduced cap and (ii) a shortened survival period, layered on the existing Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities, would materially erode the client's indemnity protection while the (iii) MAE carve-out would separately dilute the client's closing protection for the very regulatory risk already bargained for. Conceding the basket conversion (per instruction) gives the counterparty a market-standard, pro-buyer concession without meaningful downside, and is an appropriate negotiating chip. We should hold firm on the cap, MAE carve-out, and survival terms, using the conceded basket as evidence of good-faith compromise while maintaining the position that the core risk-allocation terms are non-negotiable.

VI. CONCLUSION

We recommend the following negotiation posture, in line with the controlling deal-team instruction:
1. Indemnification cap: REJECT the reduction; COUNTER to restore the original full cap.
2. Basket: CONCEDE the deductible-to-tipping conversion (per the controlling partner instruction).
3. MAE carve-out: REJECT the broad carve-out; COUNTER to narrow it to the two Schedule 3.7-disclosed inquiries.
4. Survival period: REJECT the reduction outright; restore Exhibit B survival matrix — treat as a walk-away issue per the controlling instruction.

We are prepared to prepare a response redline implementing the recommendations above and to negotiate these points with counterparty counsel.

[End of Memorandum]
